title: ASO vs. PEO: Guide to Differences, Costs and How to Choose
body_markdown:
When businesses start looking for HR support, two terms often come up: ASO and PEO. **And if you're wondering what the difference is, you're not alone.** While there are a variety of factors that make them different, the biggest difference comes down to co-employment.


A[PEO](https://www.trinet.com/peo) works through a co-employment relationship, while an[ASO](https://www.trinet.com/hr-plus) supports HR administration without becoming a co-employer. That structural difference shapes how benefits, payroll taxes, workers' compensation, and HR administration are supported.


This guide explains how each model works, how costs are typically structured, and how to decide which level of service might be the best fit for your business.


## ASO vs. PEO Simplified


The easiest way to compare an ASO and a PEO is to look at the different functions each performs.


**Here's a side-by-side look at how ASOs and PEOs compare:**


Type of Service ASO (Administrative Services Organization) PEO (Professional Employer Organization)


Business relationship


The business is the sole employer


The business enters a co-employment relationship with the PEO


Benefits


The business sponsors and administers its own benefit plans, with administrative support can be provided by the ASO


The PEO provides access to large-group benefits


Payroll taxes


Payroll taxes are filed under the business's own EIN


PEO generally processes payroll and reports wages and payroll taxes under its FEIN, subject to the applicable arrangement and service agreement


Workers' compensation


The business generally maintains its own coverage, though the ASO may help provide administrative services


The PEO typically provides access to and administers workers’ compensation coverage, depending on the PEO arrangement and service agreement


Typical pricing structure


Often a flat per-employee administrative fee for selected services


Often a flat per employee per month for administrative fees and benefits as a separate line item. Some PEOs bundle everything (administration, benefits, payroll taxes) as a percentage of payroll


Typical Business profile


Businesses that want HR administrative support while sponsoring their own benefits


Businesses that want a broader, full-service HR bundle, access to large-group benefits, risk mitigation, and shared administrative responsibility depending on the service agreement


Both models can help businesses manage HR more effectively. They just do it in different ways. An ASO keeps the business as the sole employer for payroll tax purposes and provides HR administration and expertise alongside your team members. A PEO and its client are in a co-employment relationship where certain employer-related responsibilities allocated between the client and the PEO under the client service agreement.


## What is an ASO?


An ASO, or Administrative Services Organization, provides expertise and HR administration support such as payroll processing, payroll tax administration, benefits administration, HR best practice guidance, and compliance support. With an ASO, businesses retain control over their workforce, benefits strategy, and company culture while gaining access to HR expertise, payroll administration, compliance and employee support.


Payroll taxes are filed under the company's EIN and the employer sponsors its own benefit plans, allowing it to maintain its existing provider relationships and decision-making authority.


[TriNet HR Plus](https://www.trinet.com/hr-plus) is TriNet's ASO, designed for businesses that want access to comprehensive HR technology, administrative support, and **access to** dedicated HR expertise while being the employer of record for payroll tax purposes.


## What does an ASO help handle?


An ASO can help with many of your day-to-day HR functions, depending on the provider and services selected. Common areas of support include:


**Payroll processing and payroll tax administration:** Support with payroll, payroll tax administration, and related workflows for payroll processed withing the ASO platform


**Benefits administration:** Delivers benefits support and administrative support while enabling the business to maintain control of its benefits programs and strategy.


[HR best practice guidance and compliance](https://www.trinet.com/insights/risk-management-in-hr-outsourcing) support: Access to HR support, best practices, templates, and information that can help the business manage HR more confidently.


**HR technology:** Tools that help automate and streamline HR tasks, employee data, payroll workflows, reporting, and benefits administration.


An ASO can provide specialized expertise across HR, payroll, benefits administration, and compliance. Paired with comprehensive technology, this support helps streamline day-to-day operations, allowing businesses to managing their employees and benefits programs while benefiting from trusted best practices and administrative assistance.


## What is a PEO?


A PEO, or Professional Employer Organization, provides small and medium-size businesses with a holistic HR solution through a[co-employment](https://www.trinet.com/insights/what-is-a-peo) relationship. The PEO often bundles the following services into a single solution: payroll services, access to benefits (health, retirement, voluntary), workers' compensation, compliance support, risk management support, HR best practice guidance, and HR technology.


## How does a PEO work?


A PEO provides services through a co-employment relationship. In this arrangement, the business retains control of its employees, while the PEO takes on certain employer-related responsibilities as defined in the service agreement.


For example, a PEO may process payroll based on client-provided information, report wages under the PEO's FEIN, remit and report payroll taxes for payroll processed in the PEO platform, provide access to large-group health and welfare benefits, help administer workers' compensation, and provide HR best practice guidance and compliance support. The exact responsibilities depend on the PEO and the terms of the service agreement.


[One common misconception](https://www.trinet.com/insights/peo-myths) is that a business loses control of its workforce when it works with a PEO. The businesses continue to direct and control the workforce, including decisions about hiring, compensation, schedules, performance management, discipline, terminations, workplace culture, and day-to-day operations.


Some PEOs may also be certified by the IRS or accredited by independent agencies such as the Employer Services Assurance Corporation. These designations can involve additional disclosures, certifications, requirements, or bonding obligations.

## ASO vs. PEO costs


ASO and PEO pricing can look different because the models include different levels of service and responsibility.


ASOs typically price their services as an administrative fee based on the services selected, often on a per-employee per month (PEPM) basis. PEOs may charge an administrative fee priced per employee per month (PEPM) or as a percentage of payroll. Depending on the arrangement, charges for employee benefits, workers’ compensation, payroll taxes and optional services may be separate from the administrative fee. Because pricing and included services vary by provider and client circumstances, businesses should compare the full scope of services and total costs under each proposal.


## What about HRO?


[Human Resources Outsourcing](https://www.trinet.com/faqs/hr-outsourcing-faqs) , or HRO, is a broader term for outsourcing HR functions to a third-party provider. The functions typically covered include payroll, benefits administration, HR consulting, recruiting support, compliance support, or other administrative services. ASOs and PEOs are both types of HR outsourcing models. The difference is that an ASO supports HR administration while the business remains the sole employer, and a PEO provides a broader bundled service model through co-employment.


## How to choose between an ASO and a PEO


The right model depends on how your business wants to manage HR, benefits, employer-related responsibilities, and administrative complexity. Neither model is better outright. The better fit depends on your priorities.


### An ASO may be a good fit if your business wants to:


- Remain the employer of record for payroll tax purposes for its workforce.
- Receive expert best practice guidance on payroll, benefits administration, HR documentation, and related tasks.
- Maintain more direct control over benefits strategy and vendor relationships.
- Access comprehensive HR and payroll technology.
- **Either doesn't want to offer benefits or wants to sponsor** **its** own **business-provided** benefits.


### A PEO may be a good fit if your business wants to:


- Access a comprehensive HR bundle through one provider.
- Gain access to[large-group benefits](https://www.trinet.com/insights/small-business-health-plan-options) through the PEO relationship.
- Share or allocate certain employer responsibilities through a co-employment model.
- Get support with payroll tax administration, workers' compensation administration, HR best practice guidance, and risk management.
- Support growth across states with a more comprehensive HR infrastructure.


**Businesses may be able to transition from a PEO to an ASO or vice versa as their needs change, although the transition may involve payroll tax reporting and other considerations.**


## Find the HR model that fits your business


Running HR can be a lot for a small or growing team to manage alone. **But you don't have to figure it out by yourself.** ASOs and PEOs both exist to help businesses get support, they just do **it** through different structures.


TriNet supports both paths:[TriNet HR Plus](https://www.trinet.com/hr-plus) for businesses looking for an ASO model, and[TriNet PEO](https://www.trinet.com/peo) for businesses looking for a co-employment model. Understanding the difference can help you choose the approach that best fits how your business wants to run HR.


## Frequently Asked Questions


What are the benefits of using a PEO for compliance support?


A PEO can help support compliance efforts by providing HR expertise, payroll tax administration, workers' compensation administration, and employment-related best practices. In a co-employment relationship, certain employer-reflated responsibilities are allocated between the PEO and the client through a service agreement.


Because PEOs work with many businesses, they may also help clients navigate changing federal, state, and local employment requirements and provide tools, policies, documentation, and support that may help reduce administrative burden and mitigate risk. **With a PEO, you gain** access to compliance experts and best practice guidance across HR, payroll, payroll tax, and benefits.


Is an ASO or a PEO better for a small business?


Neither model is better for every small business. An ASO may be a better fit for a business that wants to remain the employer of record for payroll tax purposes, sponsor its own benefit plans, and get help with HR administration. A PEO may be a better fit for a business that wants access to a comprehensive bundled HR solution, including access to large-group benefits through co-employment.


Can a company switch from an ASO to a PEO?


Yes. Businesses may move from an ASO to a PEO, or from a PEO to an ASO, as their needs change, subject to the applicable service agreement, payroll tax reporting requirements and other considerations. The timing and implications of any transition should be evaluated based on the business’s specific circumstances.


Does an ASO handle payroll taxes?


An ASO can support payroll tax administration depending on service agreement and, for payroll processed through the ASO platform, payroll tax filings are reported under the business's own EIN. In a PEO relationship, payroll taxes are typically reported under the PEO's FEIN, for payroll processed in the PEO platform, depending on the service agreement.
